# Results — Study 173 (Four-Percent-Rule) on real Shiller tape

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py).  One recipe — the retiree
withdraws 4% of the initial portfolio (inflation-adjusted, so a constant real dollar amount)
annually from a 60% equity / 40% bond mix, rebalanced yearly.  We run every historical
rolling 30-year cohort available in Shiller monthly data back to 1872 and ask: what
fraction survived?  What is the true safe withdrawal rate (SWR)?  Who were the near-misses,
and why?  As-of **2026-06-15**.*

## Data stamp

| Source | Window | Fingerprint |
|---|---|---|
| Shiller S&P 500 (equity real total return) | 1872–2022 | `96a5d81258d3` |
| Shiller long-rate bond proxy (real return)  | 1872–2022 | `96a5d81258d3` |

**Shiller real equity total return** = monthly real price appreciation + real dividend
(Real Dividend / 12 / Real Price), compounded annually.  **Shiller bond real return** =
modified-duration approximation (−9 × Δrate/12 + coupon/12 − CPI inflation), annual.
Long-run mean: equity **8.44%/yr real**, bond **2.46%/yr real**; equity vol **18.0%**.
N cohorts = **122** rolling 30-year windows (start years 1872–1993, each ending at t+30).

*Note: the Shiller bond proxy uses a 10-year modified duration approximation; it
reproduces the qualitative results from Bengen (1994) and Pfau (2010) but differs
somewhat from their exact TBill/intermediate-bond series.*

## The headline result — 4% Rule vs. history

At a 60/40 annual rebalance and 4% real withdrawal, **every single historical 30-year
cohort in the Shiller dataset survived** — a 100% success rate across 122 windows.
Bengen's (1994) original 4.15% SAFEMAX is confirmed:

| Metric | Value |
|---|---|
| N cohorts (30yr windows) | 122 |
| **Survival rate at 4% WR** | **100.0%** |
| Median terminal wealth (initial = 1.0) | **1.54×** |
| Worst terminal wealth (1966 cohort) | **0.13×** |
| Safe withdrawal rate (95% success) | **4.49%** |
| SAFEMAX (100% historical success) | **4.14%** |
| Survival rate at 5% WR | 79.5% |
| Survival rate at 6% WR | 53.3% |

The 4% rule is *conservative*: the historical SWR at 95% target success is **4.49%**
and the absolute SAFEMAX (survives every single window) is **4.14%**.  Bengen's round
number was a prudent underestimate of what history allowed.

## The survival by withdrawal rate

| Withdrawal rate | Survival (30yr) | Median terminal wealth |
|---|--:|--:|
| 3.0% | 100.0% | 2.34× |
| 3.5% | 100.0% | 1.87× |
| **4.0%** | **100.0%** | **1.54×** |
| 4.5% | 94.3% | 1.13× |
| 5.0% | 79.5% | 0.73× |
| 6.0% | 53.3% | 0.19× |

The rule does not exist above 4.49%: a single extra 0.5% over 4.0% already drops
survival to 94.3%.  The 4% number is not arbitrary — it sits just below the SWR cliff.

## The near-misses — sequence-of-returns risk bites

The 4% rule survived *everything historically*, but the worst cohort (1966 start) left
only **0.13× of initial wealth** after 30 years.  All five worst cohorts started with
bad early real equity returns in an already-elevated-PE environment:

| Start year | Terminal wealth | First-5yr equity return | Notes |
|---|--:|--:|---|
| **1966** | **0.130×** | **−0.7%/yr** | Worst near-miss; 1966–81 stagflation |
| 1969 | 0.186× | −3.0%/yr | Oil-shock decade |
| 1965 | 0.229× | +1.9%/yr | Inflation eroded real returns |
| 1968 | 0.293× | +3.7%/yr | Mediocre early returns |
| 1912 | 0.301× | +2.9%/yr | WWI bear market |

**Sequence-of-returns risk is the primary threat.** Among cohorts with above-median
first-5-year equity returns, the median terminal wealth is **2.38×**; for below-median
first-5-year equity returns it collapses to **0.97×** — the same 30-year window, the
same long-run returns, but only the *order* matters.

## PE10 quartile analysis — valuations at retirement predict terminal wealth

| PE10 quartile | N cohorts | Survival rate | Median terminal wealth |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| Q1 (cheap, low PE10) | 29 | 100% | 2.89× |
| Q2 | 28 | 100% | 1.56× |
| Q3 | 28 | 100% | 1.04× |
| Q4 (dear, high PE10) | 28 | 100% | 0.74× |

All four quartiles *survived* at 4%, but terminal wealth is almost **4× larger**
when retiring into cheap markets (Q1) vs. expensive markets (Q4).  Starting PE10 in
2021 was ~37 — historically Q4.  This does not predict failure, but it predicts a
leaner margin of safety.

## The 40-year horizon and beyond

For a 65-year-old retiree who lives to 105, a 30-year horizon is insufficient.  At
40 years the 4% rule begins to fail in Shiller history:

| Horizon | Survival at 4% WR | SWR at 95% success |
|---|--:|--:|
| 20 years | 100.0% | >6% |
| 30 years | 100.0% | 4.49% |
| 40 years | 94.6% | 3.97% |

At 40 years the SWR drops below 4%.  Longer-lived retirees should use a lower rate
or a dynamic spending rule.

## Why Pfau's fragility argument holds

The real Shiller mean equity return is **8.44%/yr** — the fertile soil Bengen's rule
was born in.  In a synthetic "low-yield world" with equity real return of 3% and bond
real return of 0.5% (plausible given 2024 valuations), the 95%-success SWR collapses
to **~2.0%** — half of Bengen's number.  The 4% rule is not wrong for the *past*;
it is fragile as a *forward-looking* prescription in a world of compressed real returns.

## Verdict

- **Signal — REAL.** 100% historical US survival at 4% (n = 122 cohorts); SAFEMAX
  4.14%; SWR at 95% = 4.49%.  HAC inference is not the right tool for this study
  (there is no "t-stat" on binary survival); the pattern is the result.
- **Tradability — FRAGILE.** Historically validated but fragile along three dimensions:
  (1) sequence-of-returns risk (worst cohort near 0 after 30yr); (2) today's elevated
  CAPE (PE10 ~37 in 2021, Q4 historically → leaner terminal wealth); (3) non-US data
  and low-yield projections suggest forward SWR well below 4%.  A prudent current
  number is 3.0–3.5%, not 4%.
- **Survives a long life? — FRAGILE.** At 40 years the historical SWR falls to 3.97%.
